analysis.one_liner: Gives people the right to have websites delete personal data collected about them as children.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Commerce Committee without a hearing or a vote after being referred there in February 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the existing Children's Online Privacy Protection Act, websites aimed at kids can collect children's personal information with parental consent, but once someone turns 13 they have no way to erase it. This bill would amend that law so anyone over 13 (or their guardian) could demand that a child-directed website delete everything it collected from or about them as a child, get written confirmation it was done, and see a notice on the site explaining how to ask. Only records needed for court cases or law enforcement could be kept.
analysis.who_benefits: People who grew up online and now want their childhood data — collected from them before they could consent — permanently erased. Kids who were tracked on child-directed websites and apps, and their parents, gain a legal right to a clean slate instead of a permanent digital record that follows them into adulthood.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone whose data was collected as a child

how_it_helps.text: Gives every person over 13 the right to request deletion of personal information collected from or about them when they were under 13, overriding any parental consent given at the time.
Requires child-directed websites to post a prominent notice explaining how to request deletion, to promptly delete the data, and to send written confirmation once it is gone.
Defines deletion strictly — information must not be maintained in retrievable form and cannot be retrieved in the normal course of business — so companies cannot simply hide it.
Lets state attorneys general enforce the new deletion right against operators who refuse, by adding it to the law's state-action provision.

analysis.who_pays: Websites and online services directed to children — game, video, and app platforms, and the ad networks behind them — would bear the cost of building deletion systems, verifying requests, and losing access to childhood data they currently hold. A right to deletion only has teeth if the data has commercial value, so the main cost falls on companies that monetize children's online activity.

drawbacks.text: The bill's reach is narrow: it covers only websites directed to children, or operators who actually knew they were collecting from a child. Data collected by general-audience sites and apps — where most childhood tracking happens — is left untouched unless the operator knew the user was a child.

Enforcement depends on the FTC writing rules within a year and on companies voluntarily complying; the bill creates no new private right for individuals to sue, so a person whose deletion request is ignored would have to rely on the FTC or state attorneys general to act.

Some deleted records could have legitimate value — for example, medical, safety, or account-recovery records — though the bill does carve out data needed for court processes and law-enforcement investigations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but modest: a targeted right to erase childhood data, not a general consumer-privacy law. The main honest objection is the narrow scope and weak enforcement — it does nothing about the majority of childhood data collected on general-audience platforms, and ignored requests would depend on regulators to pursue. Still, for the data it does cover, it would eliminate a permanent record created by a child that the child never consented to.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent it to the Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on February 13, 2023, with Senators Blumenthal and Hirono as original cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
The bill's only action after referral was its committee referral; no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded in the full action history.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill expired in committee without coming to a floor vote in either chamber.
The bill would have required the FTC to write rules within one year requiring child-directed websites to accept and confirm deletion requests for data collected from anyone while they were under 13.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Online services and ad networks that collected data from children keep that data indefinitely; the families who wanted it erased got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Websites and ad networks that keep kids' data

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Illinois; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it in the Senate.

for.name: Sens. Richard Blumenthal and Mazie Hirono

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral in February 2023 and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Democrats and no one ever voted on the bill, so no real partisan line ever formed; the only recorded opposition is the committee's inaction.

industries.note: These operators would have to build deletion systems, confirm deletions in writing, and give up childhood data they currently hold — data whose value comes from keeping kids' information, which runs against the interest of the people it was collected from.

industries.industry: Ad networks and data brokers serving children's platforms
industries.note: Deletion of childhood data shrinks the profiles that make targeted advertising to minors profitable; the bill's strict definition of deletion — not retrievable in the normal course of business — would take that data out of circulation entirely.
